title: No Rest for the Wicked has been delayed to 2027, promises new beta and founders packs for early buyers to tide people over
author: Connor Makar
content:
"We're holding our games to a standard we won't compromise on".

No Rest for the Wicked - the upcoming Action RPG from Ori developer Moon Studios - has been delayed into next year. Originally intended to release into version 1.0 in October, it will instead launch in March of 2027.

This news came via a social media post from a sudden statement posted to official No Rest from the Wicked social media accounts. This statement reads as follows:

"The honest truth is that we're a small team, and we're holding our games to a standard we won't compromise on. We're close, but close isn't good enough for our full 1.O launch. The extra time will help us improve performance, tighten the class system, and polish the whole game to the standard you all deserve. We'd rather take a few more months than ship something that we know isn't quite perfect yet."

While this is surely sad news for the early adopters of No Rest for the Wicked, there is a silver lining. A new open beta test is scheduled for December, which should allow a new wave of curious onlookers a chance to check out ahead of its new release date.

In addition, anyone who buys the game before January 2027 will receive founders rewards in-game once it launches properly. PlayStation pre-orders open up in January, at which point players on that platform will get around two months to get those same rewards.

In a video released to the Moon Studios YouTube channel, studio founder Thomas Mahler offered additional insight into the situation. He describes the "mad dash" to add more content such as the class system this year. As a result, it seems as though the team didn't feel the game was ready for its scheduled release.

Ah well, although this delay does mean No Rest for the Wicked is leaping away from the nightmarish release calendar coming up this year. By dodging October it avoids clashing up against Gears of War: E-Day, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, Star Wars: Galactic Racer, and many more cool looking games. Maybe it'll be for the best?

title: As the legal hunt for the GTA 6 leaker continues, Take-Two reportedly tries another more secretive Discord subpoena, this time specifying individuals
author: Sherif Saed
content:
"It now seeks more targeted information."

Rockstar parent company Take-Two has escalated its hunt for the people behind the numerous Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks from two weeks ago. The publisher has filed a request for another subpoena, though this time it's asking the court to withhold the details from the public and keep it sealed.

The subpoena request, as reported by TorrentFreak, is the second one aimed at Discord. Take-Two previously filed subpoena requests targeting multiple companies whose products were used to store and disseminate the leaked GTA 6 footage, including Discord, Microsoft, and X. Following these filings, Discord said it had yet to be served, and that it would "evaluate the validity and scope before responding" if and when it was.

Take-Two's tactics seem to be changing a bit, as the company is now trying to keep the public from being able to see details of the subpoena. Unlike the original public subpoenas, no one outside the court will be able to learn details of the information Take-Two is seeking this time. The company was criticised for the scope and scale of the information it requested in Discord's initial subpoena, which targeted hundreds of thousands of users across several Discord servers where the GTA 6 leaks mainly circulated.

The new filing, made on 28th August, appears to have a more specific target in mind. "Take-Two has identified one additional Discord user and obtained additional identifying information for a previously identified Discord user, as well as additional information concerning the community services identified in its prior subpoena for which it now seeks more targeted information," it reads.

As TorrentFreak's report shows, the targets of the subpoena are completely redacted, likely a result of its narrower focus. It's also possible the alarmed public reaction to the details of the original Discord subpoena played a role. Take-Two, of course, justified its request to keep it sealed as a way of preventing leakers from being tipped off.

At the time of writing, the subpoena has not yet been issued, and though the document remains sealed, a judge has yet to approve the request to keep it that way. If a judge does not grant that request, the "highly sensitive, confidential information" contained within may be available to view.

The GTA 6 leaks ceased shortly before the debut of Netflix's extended GTA 6 gameplay showcase. It is believed the leakers used the gameplay footage as a means of inflating the value of bespoke crypto currency and have cashed out, making off with about $270,000 (~£200,000).

title: The Blockbuster Audacity of “Hope”
author: @NewYorker
content:
At the start of the giddily entertaining monster movie “Hope,” the director and screenwriter Na Hong-jin serves up a load of bull. No, really. We’re on the South Korean side of the Demilitarized Zone, and a large male bovine has been found slashed to death near an open field. Flies buzz over the rotting carcass, which is riven by claw marks so unnaturally deep that no one can determine whomauledit. A bear? Unlikely. Maybe, one man suggests, it was that tiger from the north—the one that, flouting the rules of peninsular diplomacy, often steals across the border in search of food. This is a joke, but a telling one; the characters in this movie are used to living on high alert. The small town that they inhabit may be called Hope Harbor, but it exists in an everyday purgatory of barbed-wire fences, undetonated land mines, and signs urging residents to “report spies” and “protect the nation against infiltration.” Who could have guessed that their worst enemy would hail not from across the border but from the skies?

The people of Hope Harbor don’t know it yet, but an alien invasion is under way—and Na, a horror-thriller maximalist of uncommon patience, takes his time breaking the news. Subscribing to Spielberg’s law, definitively proved in “Jaws” (1975), that the predators we don’t see are the ones that scare us the most, the director spends the first of this movie’s two and a half hours methodically setting the scene—which, in this case, means laying waste to the scenery. Rattled by the mystery of the bull, Bum-seok (Hwang Jung-min), the bumbling, trigger-happy police chief of Hope Harbor, drives back into town and is confronted with a disaster zone. “A freaking huge monster,” in the words of an irascible eyewitness, has torn through the village, gutting shops and homes and leaving bodies strewn amid the rubble. The cinematographer, Hong Kyung-pyo (“Burning,” “Parasite”), slows the camera to an ominous crawl as Bum-seok draws his weapon and tiptoes through the debris: broken beams, caved-in ceilings, bloodstained tiles, and piles upon piles of precious, ordinary, soon to be forgotten stuff. Admirers of Na’s previous films, none more bewitchingly bonkers than “The Wailing” (2016), will recognize the cluttered crime-scene handiwork of his longtime production designer, Lee Hwok-young. Buildings, like bodies, have innards, too.

There’s a dread-soaked wit to the movie’s drawn-out approach, especially in this first hour. We may think that we’re seeing the aftermath of a creature’s rampage, but we are, in fact, being introduced to the creature itself: we are what we destroy, Na seems to be saying. From this particular trail of devastation, we can deduce that the perpetrator is colossal, fast, and possessed of a strange mix of clumsiness and stealth. As Bum-seok zeroes in on his target, Na lures us into a crafty game of predator peekaboo; we can track the monster’s proximity through the explosions that it triggers in the vicinity and the lethal projectiles that it lobs from afar. Na is so good at this brand of menace by misdirection that, by the time you finally lay eyes on the monster, you might wish you hadn’t. For one thing, the creature, whom the end credits call Va’migere (and who is played, via performance-capture technology, by Cameron Britton), is properly fearsome to behold: an unjolly green giant that chases after Bum-seok on all fours, shrieks like an emphysemic banshee, and generally brings to mind the love child of the Incredible Hulk and “The Exorcist” ’s Regan MacNeil. But it is also, deflatingly, a computer-generated creepy-crawly, and unlike some other movie monsters—say, the amphibious kidnapper from “The Host” (2006) or the sharp-eared stalkers from “A Quiet Place” (2018)—Va’migere has a humanoid face and form, rendered with an almost hyperreal incongruity. It might have wandered, or crashed, into the movie from a decade-old zombie-apocalypse video game.

Na’s solution to this problem is speed: the faster he can keep his aliens moving—Va’migere, alas, is not alone—the less likely we are to scrutinize the malevolent jumble of pixels they are. The film’s first chase is a tour de force of kinetic delirium: Sung-ae (Hoyeon), a brave junior cop, drives Bum-seok through the streets of Hope Harbor, with Va’migere sprinting furiously after them. Hong, favoring a backward-facing view of the mayhem, shoots in lengthy takes that swerve and snake with rough-and-tumble precision; the energies of car and camera seem to fuse into one. Compare this with a similarly arresting later sequence, set deep within a magnificently mossy forest, where a band of hunters, led by Sung-ki (Zo In-sung, full of rascally charisma), do battle with Va’migere’s alien friends. If the street chase transplanted “Bullitt” to the D.M.Z., this earthier showdown, which puts Sung-ki and his fellow-fighters on horseback, has the verdant majesty of a woodland Western.

Here and elsewhere, Na stretches out the action to an almost luxuriant degree, and he makes a virtue of attenuation: a run-and-gun stunt that seems repetitive the third time is somehow smashing on the eighth. It helps that the aliens are almost as hard to kill as Wile E. Coyote, and, indeed, should you emerge from “Coyote vs. Acme” with your craving for comic violence unsated, you might consider going straight into “Hope,” which is something of a live-action cartoon writ large. (There’s a touch of the Tasmanian Devil to the way Va’migere crashes through walls, leaving behind vaguely Va’migere-shaped holes.) Yet Na also insists on treating his aliens as objects of contemplation and pathos—reflections of our own misshapen humanity. In one slow-motion scene, we peer into Va’migere’s wraithlike visage and see not just rage or monstrosity but an all too relatable terror. We are what we destroy.

All four of Na’s features were shown at the Cannes Film Festival, but “Hope” was his first to appear in the main competition. Predictably, its selection triggered the kind of reflexive critical grumbling that often ensues when a gory genre movie, be it “Oldboy,” “Drive,” or “The Substance,” is elevated to the highest of world-cinema pedestals. For some of us, though, Na’s upgrade seemed overdue. His films, all of which have been critically and commercially successful, have long blurred the lines between the aspirations of the art house and the pleasures of the grind house. I still can’t shake the grisly final moments of “The Chaser” (2009), a blisteringly cynical police procedural that takes a hammer to the mere notion of competence or integrity in law enforcement. Na’s films are propelled by brutal individual acts, but they also swarm with systemic rot. His finest movie, “The Yellow Sea” (2011), strands a debt-ridden Korean Chinese immigrant in the midst of a mob war, forcing him to run and run—and kill and kill—in order to survive. It’s bleak as hell; it’s also exhilarating.

“Hope,” which is Na’s first film in a decade, represents both a step up in ambition and a step down in finesse. The movie has a goofy, galumphing beauty; it’s a bigger, dumber, shinier object than its predecessors, yet it also manifests the crudely violent small-town comedy that is one of Na’s signatures. The people of Hope Harbor speak almost exclusively in barked expletives and insults, and nearly all of them are packing serious heat; Bum-seok’s irritation at the sheer glut of unregistered weapons becomes a sly running gag. One colorful customer spouts a fabulously ripe monologue about how the aliens nearly caught him mid-defecation—a close encounter of the turd kind. More disquietingly, several of Na’s characters seem at least as fond of the art of disembowelment as their alien overlords are: witness an overeager coroner merrily firing up a chainsaw as she tackles her first alien autopsy, or a village doofus (Eum Moon-suk) whose unfortunate taste for taxidermy may have set this entire tragedy in motion.

Whom, exactly, are we supposed to root for here? Bum-seok, Sung-ae, and Sung-ki do find a shambolic Hawksian unity, after a fashion; Sung-ae, in particular, has only to step out of a car with a military-grade rifle to elicit spontaneous applause. But Na’s most interesting countermove is to seed the enemy ranks with Hollywood actors, including Michael Fassbender, Alicia Vikander, and Taylor Russell—not that you’re likely to recognize them under their gobs of shape-shifting C.G.I. Belatedly, Fassbender and Vikander, sweetly cast as a sort of alien couple, are given the most soulful lines in the entire picture, though whether soul is called for is unclear; a script that boasts a five-minute soliloquy about diarrhea is suddenly rife with mythical earnestness and impenetrable last-minute world-building. Is Na, in merging unforgettable spectacle and unutterable dialogue, laying claim to the mantle of “Avatar”-era James Cameron? Does he yearn to put the “Na” in Na’vi? Perhaps this saga of planetary conquest is also a sly commentary on Hollywood imperialism, in which even the most far-flung of small-town tales must be overwhelmed by big-name stars in visual-effects drag. Na has clearly succumbed to the blockbuster mentality: as he confirmed at Cannes, a sequel is already written. Could the next movie begin to make sense of its predecessor’s hilarious and confounding final minutes? Hope springs eternal. ♦

title: “Days and Nights in the Forest” Emerges from the Shadows
author: @NewYorker
content:
Four city jerks, privileged and frustrated young men from Kolkata, head to the countryside for a few days of slothful rest and rowdy dissipation. They approach the locals arrogantly, seeing the region’s poverty as a source for cheap, subservient help and an open field for heedless riot, but a series of chance encounters—and romantic entanglements—sends them home shaken and humbled, though maybe not wiser. This is the premise of Satyajit Ray’s 1970 melodrama “Days and Nights in the Forest,” which had long been hard to see until the release, earlier this year, of a 4K restoration, which has now arrived on the Criterion Channel. (It will also be released by the Criterion Collection, on Blu-ray and DVD, on September 29th.) The film is a teeming, turbulent, confrontational meld of emotion and observation, placing the eruptive pressure of societal conflict amid the seeming trivia of social life.

“Days and Nights in the Forest” is based on an autobiographical novel by Sunil Gangopadhyay, published in 1968. The feature’s literary basis is underlined when two of the men reminisce about a literary journal they founded long ago, but it’s palpable throughout, in the freewheeling actions and impulsive dialogue, which Ray nonetheless films with analytical detachment and gimlet scrutiny—as befits a work of personal experience that, however, isn’t his own but the author’s. (Ray’s critical distance from the characters is as crucial to the movie’s emotional power as is his wide-ranging empathy.) The movie’s anecdotal aspect both abstracts and expands the drama. Ray’s incremental approach to the story elides through lines and plot mechanisms in such a way that the crisscrossing relationships and events form an intellectual map of the forces underlying them.

From the start, there’s something dubiously bookish—callow and potentially callous—about the four men’s rustic jaunt. As Ashim (Soumitra Chatterjee), who planned the excursion, drives, Sanjoy (Subhendu Chatterjee) reads to the others from the back seat about Palamu, the region where they’re headed. The book he’s reading from leeringly describes the locale’s women as dark-skinned and scantily clad; the four men’s minds are on sex and love. They tease Hari (Samit Bhanja), also in the back seat, about a girlfriend leaving him; he pridefully asserts that he “dumped” her, but a flashback shows what really happened. Sanjoy is similarly teased about his relationship with his boss’s daughter, another source of resentment that shows up in a flashback. Meanwhile, the hyperactive, sardonic Shekhar (Rabi Ghosh), riding shotgun, is unemployed and claims to have no time for the “bourgeois” frivolity of romance.

The melodramatic force of Ray’s film is built into these spare but potent character sketches. Douglas Sirk, Hollywood’s supreme director of melodramas and a theoretician of the genre, spoke of his films’ dependence on the contrast between “immovable” characters and “split” ones. In “Days and Nights in the Forest,” Hari and Sanjoy, in the back seat, are the “split” characters, their flashbacks revealing the division between their present-tense façades and their bitterly remembered realities. Sitting up front, Ashim, who is coolly brazen, and the antic, unreflective Shekhar—the king and the jester—are the “immovable” ones, with unified identities that are nonetheless exposed and vulnerable.

All four are manifestly bourgeois, flashing their cash from the moment they arrive at the village where they are to stay. They blusteringly order a bedraggled local man named Lakha to accompany and serve them. (“Ask if he can come with us,” Sanjoy says to Ashim in English, certain that Lakha won’t understand.) They arrive as self-aware screwups, who know full well that they should have reserved their bungalow in advance but instead hector and bribe the guesthouse’s beleaguered watchman into bending the rules and giving them one anyway. He fears he’ll be fired for it, and one of the travellers—again in English—quips, “Thank God for corruption.”

The men are keen to go slumming. At night, they go drinking at a shedlike bar where women, to their surprise, drink together as heavily as men do. One of the women, Duli (Simi Garewal), noticing the haughty and higher-class men sizing her and her friends up, boldly approaches them for drinking money. The next morning, when the men show up at the local market in search of breakfast, a group of women, including Duli, are there in search of day labor. The men hire three, including Duli, to do their chores. One woman is pressed into service as a punkah wallah, charged with pulling a rope that keeps a hinged ceiling fan flapping back and forth and keeping the men cool. As for Duli, she sweeps the bungalow’s floor with a whisk broom, Hari ogling her as she bends over.

But Hari’s friends have other pursuits in mind. Shekhar brazenly asks Lakha where they can find “middle-class women,” and the poor man obediently points the way. As the four men walk the designated road, they pass a badminton court, where they encounter two women of the local gentry: Rini (Sharmila Tagore), a young, unmarried woman of intellectual ambition and poetic refinement, and her sister-in-law, Jaya (Kaberi Bose), a still youthful widow who is desperately lonely and the mother of a lively young boy. Surprised to encounter urbane menfolk here, the women lead them in a whirl of home visits—Rini’s father, Sadashiv (Pahari Sanyal), is a landowner—and social outings. Gradually, the women’s strong and probing personalities lay bare the weaknesses and presumptions of the ostensibly suitable men in their midst.

The men and women are instantly on familiar terms, and the push and pull of formalities and witticisms creates an atmosphere of brightness and romantic energy, although the household is darkened by tragedy and muffled by isolation. Rini guides Ashim to a small aerie that’s her solitary retreat, with her English-language books and her Western records (including “Rubber Soul” and “Joan Baez in Concert”), but their romantic connection is shadowed by her keen awareness of his cavalier, solipsistic arrogance. Jaya, with little hope of romance, seeks a sexual encounter, in a powerfully ironic scene contrasting the purity of desire with the fretful inhibitions of conventional morality.

As the story unfolds, relationships between friends, transactions with locals and bureaucrats, episodes of love and lust, and moments of painful self-awareness produce a subjective panorama of unredressed inequality, squandered energy, stifling tradition, and a restive quest for liberation. Ray gives his four men a natural exuberance and supplies them with a varied, pugnaciously expansive range of action. Whether in straightforward mealtime banalities or chatter when bathing at an outdoor well, or in the raucous ribaldry of their drunken rambles, they bring high spirits and a hunger for experience, albeit on their own presumptuous terms. Ray approaches the action with a vigorous yet reflective and piercingly probing eye. Observing the four men at the bar, his camera tracks from face to face, pausing at each before passing on, making palpable both connections and disconnections—isolation amid the overheated tumult.

The movie’s romantic centerpiece is a party game that the two women teach the four men during a picnic. It’s a memory game, in which the group sits in a circle, one member says the name of a famous person, and the next one repeats that name and adds another, and so on; those who forget a name are out, until a winner remains. For many movie lovers seeing the film for the first time, the game will be startlingly familiar, as it was more recently played in Wes Anderson’s “Asteroid City,” by a group of scientifically precocious teen-agers. (For that matter, the setup of Ray’s film also prefigures that of Anderson’s “The Darjeeling Limited.”) For both Ray and Anderson—who was involved in the current restoration and is a long-standing admirer of Ray’s—the demanding game gives rise to high drama and keen suspense along with tender comedy and rapturous romanticism. Both directors make use of its patterned and repetitive format to embody emotional extremes in a precise and formalized array of visual imagination.

The trivial outcome of this friendly competition plays an outsized role in the relationship of Rini and Ashim—a psychological wrangle in which the discerning Rini has the upper hand and lets him know it. (Ray films their climactic confrontation in intense, dual closeups, framed starkly against the sky, that are as indiscreetly intimate as they are sculpturally grand.) There’s another struggle, between Hari and Duli, that’s altogether more troubling, because of the inherent inequality of the relationship—between an educated middle-class man and a desperately poor and unworldly woman of doubtless little schooling who is also in his employ. Ray pays close attention to the fine points of the abusive relationship—including the confusion of emotion and the bedrock of money—and he situates it at the violent edge of class conflict and stifled revolt.

“Days and Nights in the Forest” came near the midpoint of Ray’s career. By 1970, he’d made more than a dozen features since his Neo Realist-inspired début, “Pather Panchali,” from 1955 (the first entry in his Apu trilogy, completed in 1959), and his work ranged from the historicist formalism of “The Music Room” to the ferocious urban feminism of “The Big City” to the time-shifting political modernism of “The Hero” to the antic musical fantasy of “The Adventures of Goopy and Bagha.” (He made his final dramatic feature in 1991, at the age of sixty-nine, the year before his death.) With “Days and Nights in the Forest,” he varies tones and moods widely within one drama as if also turning inward, considering urban intellectuals’ distance from India at large, the differences of experience, background, and identity that make connections either a struggle or an exploitation. His four city dwellers head home with more than just wounds. They bear symbolic souvenirs, physical and verbal, that they, like viewers, ignore at their own moral risk. ♦

title: Why the Lindsay Clancy Trial Ended in a Deadlock
author: @NewYorker
content:
Some sort of resolution to the Lindsay Clancy trial seemed finally within reach on Thursday afternoon when, after six days of deliberations and two reports of deadlock, word came from the jury room. It wasn’t a verdict but an apparent complaint about a holdout. The foreperson wrote that a single juror was refusing to follow instructions from the judge, William Sullivan, on the standard for proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Clancy, who was on trial for murdering her three young children, had pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. The note itself wasn’t made public, but Kevin Reddington, Clancy’s defense attorney, said that it “clearly and unequivocally” showed an 11–1 split, with the lone juror blocking an acquittal. Reddington immediately asked Judge Sullivan to remove the dissenting juror, and a long, heated scrum followed at the bench. As lawyers crowded in, Reddington could be seen slapping down a sheaf of papers. Clancy, who was left paralyzed by a suicide attempt that followed the killings, was brought forward in her wheelchair to listen. Prosecutors argued that the jury’s dispute reflected not misconduct but a legitimate disagreement over the evidence. Judge Sullivan questioned the jurors one by one, removed none, and, on Friday morning, over the defense’s objections, refused to investigate further. Shortly before noon, after thirty-eight hours of deliberation, the jury returned a final message. “With a heavy heart,” it read, they still had not managed to come to a verdict. Reddington filed an emergency appeal seeking to block a mistrial, but the effort failed, and Judge Sullivan declared one anyway.

It should come as no surprise that the jurors had trouble reaching unanimity. Five weeks of nationally televised testimony, from more than eighty witnesses, did not settle the central question: What was going through the defendant’s mind when she killed her kids? The prosecution and the defense never disagreed about the case’s basic facts. One evening in January of 2023, after sending her husband out to pick up dinner, Clancy fatally strangled Cora, who was five, Dawson, who was three, and Callan, who was eight months old, in the basement of the family’s home in Duxbury, Massachusetts; then she cut her neck and wrists and jumped from a second-floor window. The jury was asked to determine whether Clancy, a labor-and-delivery nurse who’d been in the midst of a well-documented mental-health crisis, should be exempt from criminal responsibility under Massachusetts law, either because she lacked the capacity to understand that what she was doing was wrong or because she was unable to stop herself from doing it.

Day after day, Judge Sullivan ordered jurors to ignore press coverage and commentary on social media, where self-appointed sleuths combed through testimony, diagnosed Clancy from afar, and seized on minor inconsistencies to construct a baseless theory that her husband was the culprit. The jury could hardly have missed the divisive displays outside the courthouse. Pink-clad Clancy supporters gathered by the dozens, holding up placards that read “COMPASSION BEFORE JUDGMENT” and “LISTEN TO MOTHERS,” while a smaller counter-presence carried signs of its own: “REMEMBER THE REAL VICTIMS”; “KIDSLAUGHTER.” As testimony came to a close, the judge granted a request from the defense to include involuntary manslaughter as a possible verdict, giving jurors an option in between convicting Clancy of murder and finding her not guilty by reason of insanity. In the end, though, there was apparently no compromise to be found.

In most states, defendants bear the burden of proving their insanity. In Massachusetts, it falls to prosecutors to prove criminal responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt. Leading the prosecution were Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham, a pair of stolid assistant district attorneys in structured suits and dark rectangular glasses. During opening statements, Buckingham, who wore her hair pulled back with the sort of bow that she said Cora had loved, promised to reveal an “extremely controlling, meticulous, and manipulative” version of Lindsay Clancy, a sinister inverse to “pictures you’ll see of the doting mother, the dedicated nurse.” But in the course of the trial this portrait never materialized. Many of the state’s own witnesses—a pediatrician, a preschool teacher, a colleague of Clancy’s, a local friend—supplied favorable character evidence for the defense, sometimes even before Reddington rose to cross-examine them. Elaine Rossi, the family’s nanny, repeated what she’d told the state police: “I observed a wonderful mom who loved her kids.”

No witness complicated the prosecution’s case more than Clancy’s ex-husband, Patrick, who spoke of his former wife with the same sympathy that he has maintained since their children’s deaths. He recalled Clancy inventing songs for them and cooking green eggs and ham for Cora, who adored Dr. Seuss. “She was very dedicated,” Patrick said. “She did everything.” During his testimony, the prosecution produced a spiral notebook in which Clancy had left instructions for caretakers on when to put down the baby, which vegetables to prepare for dinner, how to cut up the sweet potatoes. Was all this meant to conjure an insidiously controlling mother? Patrick testified, “I would’ve done the same.”

To supply a motive, the prosecutors tried to assemble evidence that Clancy had simply soured on family life. They got Christopher Clancy, Patrick’s father, to allow that, at Thanksgiving, she’d grown “a little frustrated” when one of her children wouldn’t be seated for dinner. They introduced a much discussed Facebook post, written a year and a half before the killings, in which Clancy had called Dawson, who was then nineteen months old, “the most difficult human I have ever encountered.” More than once, though, the prosecutors appeared oblivious of where their own lines of inquiry would lead. They confronted Patrick with text messages about an anniversary trip that he’d arranged a month or so before the killings, as if to contest his account of the family’s crisis, only for him to clarify that the plans were scrapped because Lindsay was too unwell to go. They held up prescription bottles still filled with pills, to suggest that she hadn’t been taking the medication she blamed for her deterioration, just for Reddington to haul out a bag containing empty bottles that the police had overlooked in a nightstand drawer.

Sprague seemed most self-assured when she pulled on latex gloves to lift the grimmest exhibits out of evidence bags: the clothes that the children were found in—Cora’s pink robe, Dawson’s dinosaur underwear, Callan’s snowflake-printed onesie—and the exercise bands that their mother had used to strangle them. But even the urge to keep jurors trained on the brute horror of the killings could get the better of the prosecution. While cross-examining Sue Clancy, Patrick’s mother, about the deaths of her grandchildren, Buckingham established that Sue was an active member of the Catholic Church, then asked, “So you’re aware that murder is considered a mortal sin?” Before Sue could answer, the defense objected, Judge Sullivan banged his gavel, and the question was stricken from the record.

The prosecution wasn’t alone in straining for a tidier story than the evidence could sustain. Reddington, a beetle-browed veteran trial lawyer with a restlessly combative style, worked to cast Clancy as a casualty of the psychiatric establishment, misdiagnosed by doctor after doctor and fobbed off with a succession of thirteen hastily prescribed medications. As testimony showed, though, Clancy was never on more than two or three prescriptions at once, and she chose to stop several antidepressants well before they could have taken effect. According to medical records, she acknowledged to the psychiatrist Jennifer Tufts, “I keep reaching out to different people and not sticking with the plan.” Reddington’s cross-examinations of Clancy’s health-care providers yielded less and less as the trial progressed. At one point, he made a show of close reading Tufts’s notes to suggest that she’d recorded and then ignored a possible sign of bipolar disorder. (She hadn’t; Reddington’s argument hinged on an ambiguous comma.) The defense faulted Clancy’s providers for missing this particular diagnosis, but Rebecca Jollotta, a psychiatric nurse practitioner who took over Clancy’s care, testified that she had raised the possibility herself, at an appointment that Patrick attended. As Jollotta recalled, he interrupted her to say, “My wife is not bipolar,” and Clancy said nothing.

The haphazard trajectory of Clancy’s treatment does leave one to wonder how she might have fared with regular talk therapy and earlier inpatient care—both of which her providers had recommended—or with fewer prescriptions, better coördination among hospital systems, and a safety plan that accounted for the small but real risk of filicide. Three weeks before the killings, Clancy voluntarily admitted herself to McLean Hospital, a renowned psychiatric facility outside Boston. After five days, she asked to be discharged so that she could attend her daughter’s birthday party. Keeping her there against her will would have been a drastic intervention, permissible by law only if doctors believed that she was likely to cause serious harm. But Clancy’s medical providers had a limited view of the danger. She’d told them that she was having suicidal ideations but consistently denied having a plan to kill herself, and though she’d told her mother and Patrick about thoughts of harming her children she never disclosed those thoughts to a doctor. Reddington had to talk around this impasse, badgering Clancy’s providers about matters such as their use of telemedicine, as though this wasn’t standard practice. “So you couldn’t give her a hug, could you?” he asked Tufts, apparently trying to brand her as callous. She replied, coolly, “That’s not actually something that psychiatrists typically do.”

Clancy’s trial has generated the most intense national conversation about postpartum mental health in recent memory. Many commentators have, fairly, lamented that it has taken such a horrific tragedy to raise awareness of the issue; they point out that the kinds of struggles Clancy experienced are both common and underdiagnosed (roughly one in eight new mothers reported symptoms of postpartum depression in a recent survey), even if the actions she took are exceedingly rare. That Clancy was universally thought of as an excellent mother and an authority on infants—not to mention that her family was white, photogenic, and comfortably suburban—made her a potent symbol. If this could happen to a woman so seemingly with-it and well resourced—one with adequate insurance, months of maternity leave, medical expertise, a husband who worked from home, supportive in-laws a few towns over, and parents ready to drive in from out of state—then what hope was there for other troubled mothers?

In the courtroom, though, the general impression of Clancy’s togetherness cut against the defense’s argument that she had lost control. Reddington struggled to marshal legible proof that she was experiencing psychosis, because none of the providers who treated her before the killings had observed signs of it. Instead, he had to account for evidence that she appeared cogent on the day in question: that she’d taken her daughter to a pediatrician’s appointment in the morning; that she’d sent Patrick to pick up dinner from a relatively distant restaurant from which they’d never ordered takeout, then added on a last-minute stop at CVS, which kept him out of the house longer; that she sounded lucid when he called from the store and she picked up, possibly in the middle of the killings; and that one of her first questions, when she awoke in the hospital, was whether she had a lawyer. The defense would have benefitted from calling a specialist in postpartum mood disorders to explain how easily psychotic symptoms can be missed in high-functioning new mothers. That testimony was expected to come from the leading perinatal psychiatrist Margaret Spinelli, who’d attended portions of the trial, but on the afternoon that she was to take the stand Judge Sullivan dismissed jurors early, citing an “unforeseen circumstance.” (Later, Spinelli was dropped from the witness list without explanation.)

Much of Reddington’s case turned on Clancy’s claim that she’d hallucinated a male voice commanding her to kill the children. The defense’s most helpful witness on this front was the forensic psychiatrist Phillip Resnick, who has spent more than half a century studying maternal infanticide. Two decades ago, Resnick helped secure a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity in the case of Andrea Yates, a Texas woman who drowned her five children in a bathtub. In Clancy’s case, Resnick testified that she’d been “frankly psychotic” in the moment of the killings, experiencing what he called a “delusion of influence”: “It was almost like she was a puppet,” he said, “and someone else was pulling the strings.” But what Clancy didn’t have, and Yates did, was a medical record documenting years of unmistakable psychotic symptoms. Although Clancy had repeatedly complained of intrusive thoughts, some about harming the children, she had never described hearing voices before the killings; nor has she reported them since.

Kirk Heilbrun, a forensic psychologist who assessed Clancy for the prosecution, testified that he is “always very careful” with symptoms that emerge only during the commission of an offense, because they provide “a convenient way of lessening your own culpability.” He added that the voice Clancy described had arrived without the kinds of delusions that usually accompany so-called command hallucinations. (Yates, for instance, was convinced that drowning her children would save them from Satan.) As prosecutors pointed out, even Resnick has written that command hallucinations are easy to fabricate, and Clancy’s own accounts of the voice were inconsistent. She told a hospital chaplain the voice had warned her that neither she nor her children would be safe unless she obeyed; she told forensic examiners that the voice had said to kill the children so that she could kill herself. She told one evaluator that the voice came on only after Patrick’s phone call from CVS, while she stood at the refrigerator preparing to make chicken nuggets. This claim, however, became a distracting point of dispute: Patrick had testified that Dawson was already eating chicken nuggets when he left the house. Such discrepancies would matter less if the voice were not so central to Clancy’s defense. But the prosecution was able to frame the voice as a mark of her unreliability rather than a sign of her illness.

To the extent that the state’s expert witnesses were credible, it was because they acknowledged what the prosecutors themselves tried to play down: that Clancy was in the grip of a serious psychiatric illness, and that her suicide attempt, which the prosecution had treated as half-hearted, was, in fact, deadly serious. Heilbrun testified that Clancy was “still in mourning for those kids,” and recalled her telling him, when he assessed her, “I have lost everything, and I don’t want to be here.” During a cross-examination of the forensic psychiatrist Gregory Saathoff, the prosecution’s final witness, Reddington read aloud the state’s pledge, from its opening statements, to expose a woman who “no longer liked the life she thought she wanted.” Saathoff replied that this characterization “really minimizes what she was going through.” By closing arguments, the prosecution had apparently absorbed the more nuanced story. “There’s no dispute that Lindsay Clancy was suffering from mental illness and that she tried to kill herself,” Sprague told the jury, as though her team hadn’t been calling both claims into question for the better part of the past three years. Now she argued that Clancy had killed the children to clear the way for her own suicide: “And I’m not saying she was happy about it,” Sprague explained. “I’m saying that it was what she had to do to end her misery. But it was a choice.”

If that is true, and Clancy chose to kill herself and take her children with her, was her act rational? Experts for both sides invoked the idea of “altruistic filicide,” a term that Resnick coined for parents who kill their children in the hope of sparing them real or imagined suffering. In his closing arguments, Reddington might have done more to follow the logic, or illogic, of that concept: Could a loving mother see strangling her children as a form of “altruism” unless her illness had substantially distorted her sense of reality? He might have sidestepped the fraught topic of the voice altogether, emphasizing instead the story of a mentally ill woman who fought horrific impulses, hallucinatory or otherwise, until they overtook her.

Throughout the televised trial, the jurors were kept off camera, but earlier this week, as the fourth day of deliberations ended, a fifty-six-year-old Clancy supporter and self-described “crime junkie” was arrested for allegedly filming them leaving the courthouse. Any jury considering this devastating case might have struggled to reach agreement, but it’s hard to imagine that the surrounding spectacle didn’t intensify divisions, making consensus more elusive. If prosecutors decide to retry Clancy, assembling an impartial jury will only be more difficult the next time around. As the case remains in the headlines, so will postpartum mental illness, but will Clancy’s story ultimately encourage women to report disturbing symptoms, or simply deepen the terror and stigma around them?

Roughly two dozen countries have statutes that classify maternal infanticide as less culpable than ordinary murder; the United States recognizes no such distinction, forcing cases like Clancy’s into the contentious framework of the insanity defense. This mistrial is one measure of how poorly that framework fits. Some people will continue to see Clancy primarily as a mother who killed her children; many others will see, above all, a woman who suffered a profound psychiatric crisis. The lingering dilemma, which may prove no easier for a future jury to resolve, is what the law should make of someone who was both.♦

title: The Current and Anxious State of Childhood
author: @NewYorker
content:
We blame smartphones—but the problem might be us.

September 4, 2026

Illustration by Josie Norton

Early in the psychologist Peter Gray’s new book, “Restoring Childhood: How to Set Kids Free in the Age of Anxiety,” he proposes a thought experiment. “Imagine that your spouse or your closest friend had the same power over you that parents typically have over children,” he suggests. Although you’re an adult, this “loving person” insists that you never leave the house without an accompanying guardian or a G.P.S. tracker. When you return, they demand a full account of what you did. Frequently, they communicate with your boss, who “controls you the way a teacher controls children at school.” This boss reprimands you for arriving even a minute late, and prohibits you from talking with your co-workers without permission; you must even ask, publicly, to use the bathroom. “Everything you do is judged and ranked in comparison to the work of your coworkers,” Gray goes on. And, when you wrap up at the office, “your employer also requires you to do more work at home,” and “encourages your loving spouse (or friend) to be sure you do that work.”

This doesn’t sound like a very nice life, does it? It’s an existence in which you’re micromanaged and surveilled, given almost no freedom or privacy, and put under constant pressure while, at the same time, being seen as incompetent and lazy. (Why else would all this have to be done to you, for your own good?) And yet, Gray argues, it’s how many children live in affluent Western countries, including the United States. Now eighty-two, Gray has spent decades studying kids, particularly how they spend their free time. In “Restoring Childhood,” he warns that they now have none, in both senses: they have no time, because they are over-scheduled and over-schooled, and their time isn’t free, because adults are neither willing nor able to leave even older kids unsupervised.

There’s a kind of book that tells you something you already know, but shows that it’s worse than you think. Samuel Moyn’s “Gerontocracy in America,” which I wrote about a few months ago, is such a book: you knew that the population was aging, but it’s a shock—and an illuminating one—to learn that the median age of a voter in a political primary is now sixty-five. “Restoring Childhood,” similarly, reveals that the slopes of familiar trend lines are steeper than you thought. In 1971, for instance, eighty-six per cent of English elementary-school children had permission to walk home from school alone; that number dropped to thirty-five per cent in 1990, and to twenty-five per cent in 2010. Child-protective services used to intervene mainly in cases of child abuse; over the decades, however, their remit grew to include not just neglect but “supervisory neglect,” a new parental offense that might involve leaving children briefly unattended in benign circumstances. Today, Gray reports, thirty-eight per cent of children will be at the center of a C.P.S. investigation at some point in their lives.

If you let your children play at the park by themselves, you could be reported by your neighbors and led away in handcuffs: it’s no wonder that many of today’s parents keep their kids on a short leash. Gray, meanwhile, describes how, at age four, he was sent to the corner store by himself to buy cigarettes, crossing the street along the way. A few years later, he joined the scrum of kids who spent their after-school time playing around the neighborhood almost entirely unsupervised. Decade by decade, he writes, the childhood he enjoyed has been replaced by a new way of growing up. And the result, he argues, has been an ongoing decline in the happiness and mental health of young people. “The ultimate goal of childhood is to break away from dependence on parents and establish oneself as one’s own person,” Gray asserts. But adults, increasingly, are building a world in which this is impossible.

The rise in documented mental-health troubles among young people is beyond doubt. Currently, about one in six American children have some sort of mental-health diagnosis; for kids older than twelve, the numbers have increased steadily since about 2010. In “The Anxious Generation,” from 2024, the social psychologist Jonathan Haidt argued that smartphones and social media are largely to blame. The book marshalled substantial scientific evidence, and reinforced the intuitions of parents dismayed by their phone-addled children. But researchers received “The Anxious Generation” more cautiously. In 2025, a team of scholars convened a hundred and twenty experts from a range of disciplines, asking them to evaluate the arguments in the book. The resulting paper—“A Consensus Statement on Potential Negative Impacts of Smartphone and Social Media Use on Adolescent Mental Health”—has a Rorschach quality. The experts were quite certain that youth mental health has declined, and that smartphones can cause sleep problems. But in many other areas they took a more middle-of-the-road view. Although the majority of experts believed that smartphones could cause “social deprivation,” for example, almost all of them also said that “both the magnitude and direction” of those effects “are likely influenced by various individual and social moderators.” In other words, a lot depends on the context and the kid. For some people, social media really is social.

It would be convenient if smartphones were the root of all evil. If that were the case, then banning them would resolve the crisis of kids’ mental health. Yet, despite the subtitle of his book—“How the Great Rewiring of Childhood Is Causing an Epidemic of Mental Illness”—Haidt, like Gray, situates the rise of the smartphone within a larger transformation in the nature of childhood, urging parents to give their children more “opportunities to exercise agency” and “pursue unsupervised adventure.” The phone question, therefore, is one of proportion. How much of the problem is attributable to the use of smartphones? How much of it might be solved by prying them from our children’s hands?

It’s notable that many studies of smartphone bans show modest effects. A recent study, published in May, found that bans in Florida middle and high schools had no substantial effect on test scores. The most encouraging study I’ve come across is “Smartphone Bans, Student Outcomes and Mental Health,” by Sara Abrahamsson, a Norwegian researcher. Her clever approach looks at a large number of middle schools in Norway, ranking their divergent smartphone policies across a range from strictness to leniency. (Some schools have no policy; others ban phones entirely; those in the middle allow students to use them sometimes.) She then compares these policies with grades and independent mental-health data from Norway’s health-care system. Abrahamsson finds that there are benefits to the bans (less bullying, better grades, and fewer mental-health consultations), that there is more benefit when they are more stringent, and that the gains are largest among girls, who use their phones more. Her most striking finding is that girls are less likely to seek mental-health care if they go to a school where phones are banned. And yet the academic gains, though real, are equivalent to the ones you might see if class size were reduced by one student. The number of mental-health appointments for girls goes down, but their rate of diagnosis doesn’t change. We might have hoped for larger effects, given the alleged power of the phone.

Gray has two theories about why such bans don’t seem to be producing bigger shifts. First, he suggests that the negative effects of smartphone use are overestimated; in fact, he goes further, arguing that phones and social media have upsides for many kids, those who find them rewarding and fun and enjoy them without having their brains “rewired.” His over-all reading of the research on phones and kids is that the devices “can have both positive and negative effects on kids’ emotions, and these can vary greatly from person to person,” such that “neither reliably trumps the other for the population of teens as a whole.” Ultimately, he sees phone use as not fundamentally dissimilar from internet use in the pre-phone era. When kids first got online, parents were bewildered and alarmed, but kids, who tend to gravitate to new technology, found freedom in a space that was basically ungoverned. Similarly, kids today use phones mainly to communicate with their friends about the incomprehensible stuff they find interesting. They gossip, fight, explore, flirt, nerd out, bully each other, and forge friendships—just like they would in person, if their parents would ever let them hang out unsupervised.

One might object, reasonably, that today’s phones, with their habit-forming social platforms and red-pilled or body-shaming influencers, are portals to a novel hellscape. But Gray’s second theory, broadly, is that of course we’d think that—we’ve lost all sense of the gulf that ought to exist between parents and children, and now take it for granted that our kids’ lives should be almost totally transparent to us, so that we can better insure that all of their activities satisfy our adult senses of propriety, safety, and usefulness. Yet independence, Gray writes, must be authentic if it’s to be learned, and risk must be actual. (He notes that kindergarteners, when presented with images of kids having fun and asked to identify “play,” tend to choose pictures with no adult in the picture.) In the old days, when parents shooed their children out of the house and let them roam around, they knew their kids might get up to no good—and that they might not find out about it. But this seemed an acceptable trade-off for a childhood in which kids quickly learned to act independently. The adults of the past, in other words, understood that kids needed to be kids, and that they could succeed in this only when adults weren’t there.

Taking this idea seriously requires believing in a now vanished world. Over the course of a chapter titled “Tightening the Leash,” Gray charts the “many intertwined changes” that have eroded “children’s freedom to play and move about independent of adult control.” There was television, which, starting in the nineteen-fifties, kept kids indoors; also, houses got a lot bigger, and families smaller, so that most kids suddenly had the option of retreating to their own bedrooms. Outside the home, adults took control of kids’ sports, replacing sandlot games with Little League and other organized, competitive, coach-centered endeavors. Housing developments increasingly omitted sidewalks, favoring drivers over walkers, and the country grew more litigious, making planners wary of playgrounds, which could attract lawsuits when kids got hurt. (“The number of lawyers in the United States per thousand citizens increased from 1.46 in 1950 to 3.9 in 2023,” Gray notes.) In the nineteen-eighties, parents grew terrified of “stranger danger,” even though most missing kids are runaways. And social norms changed: it became less common for teens to hold jobs and make their own money. (Today’s kids “are anxious about their future partly because they have reduced opportunity to experience the work world,” Gray suggests.)

An especially important change, Gray argues, was that school got more intense. Between 1950 and 2015, the average American school year got five weeks longer. Recess shrunk, and time for lunch contracted from an hour (at many schools) to twenty minutes. Academic requirements increased dramatically, even for very young children, with more time spent sitting at desks, and less time devoted to art, music, and other fun activities; a pervasive emphasis on standardized tests disheartened teachers and made schoolwork itself more boring. Meanwhile, homework piled up, eating into what remained of kids’ autonomy after school. When asked what makes them stressed, Gray observes, children don’t talk about their phones: “In every national survey I have been able to find in which school-aged kids are asked to identify the main causes of psychological distress, school pressure comes out on top by a large margin.” Adults like the idea of school, Gray concludes, and so are reluctant to criticize it. But, in his view, the discussion of mental distress among kids ought to focus there.

Who’s right, Haidt or Gray? Will banning phones bring real-world clarity and connection to kids’ lives, or deprive them of one of their last routes to autonomy in a claustrophobic world? This might strike you as a disagreement that’s unlikely to be resolved anytime soon. But, if Gray and Haidt disagree sharply, they also share a lot of common ground—in fact, until recently, they served together on the board of Let Grow, a nonprofit dedicated to “leading the movement for childhood independence.” (In The Atlantic, Kaitlyn Tiffany writes that Gray resigned from the board last year, so that the other members wouldn’t be “caught in the middle of a conflict.”) Their accounts are in competition, but are still useful together: if you find one persuasive, you ought to read the other.

Social phenomena are hard to explain. Almost always, they’re multicausal—that is, caused by a multitude of factors that swirl together. The difficulty with multicausal problems is that it’s hard to effect multipronged solutions. Suppose that Gray is right, and that today’s kids are suffering from sixty years of accumulated social, economic, and technological change. And suppose, additionally, that Haidt is also right, and that—for many kids—smartphones are deepening these problems and adding new ones. No individual person, school superintendent, or government agency can undo or mitigate all of these developments simultaneously. The best anyone can do is to choose a lever and pull it. From this perspective, the existence of disagreement is a good thing. It gives us more levers to pull. ♦

title: Judge blocks Trump's second birthright citizenship order
author: Kelsey Dallas
content:
Skip to main content

Newsletter

/Sep 3, 2026

Chief Justice William Rehnquist died on this day in 2005. He served on the court for more than 33 years, the first 14 of which he spent as an associate justice.

At the Court

Two Republican groups asked the court on its interim docket to block a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit preventing political parties and joint fundraising committees from paying preferential broadcast rates for political ads. The court has asked the four Democrats who challenged the groups’ access to more favorable rates to respond to the request by noon EDT today.

In another interim docket dispute, a Michigan group urged the court to require Michigan election officials to put on the November ballot its proposal for requiring proof of citizenship to vote in the state. Michigan officials filed their response to that request on Wednesday. Learn more about their filing in the Morning Reads section.

This Friday at 9:30 a.m. EDT, the court will release its third and final summer order list. (We discussed what these lists typically address in our July 13 newsletter.)

Morning Reads

US judge blocks Trump's newest order limiting birthright citizenship

Nate Raymond, Reuters

On Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland "blocked the Trump administration from enforcing a new executive order limiting the number of people eligible for birthright citizenship that President Donald Trump issued after the U.S. Supreme Court rejected his previous effort," according to Reuters. Boardman imposed her preliminary injunction "at the request of immigrant rights advocates who had last year secured a ruling from her blocking" Trump's first executive order on the issue on behalf of a class of babies who would have been denied citizenship under that earlier order. She cited the Supreme Court's June ruling striking down Trump's first order to explain her decision, asserting that the court had "already decided that the children in the class are citizens at birth." "Her order bars agencies including the U.S. Department of State, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, and the Social Security Administration from taking any action to interfere with, deny or fail to recognize citizenship of children covered by the class action."

New Jersey Seeks High Court Review of Kalshi Sports Markets

Gillian R. Brassil, Bloomberg Law

On Wednesday, New Jersey brought the growing battle over regulatory control of prediction markets to the Supreme Court, asking the justices “to clear up a nationwide legal debate over whether sports prediction markets offer” sports bets, which are subject to state regulation, or if instead, they host “hedging tools called ‘swaps’ that are under the purview of” the federal government, according to Bloomberg Law. New Jersey’s appeal of a ruling from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit embracing this latter view comes less than a week after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit sided with Nevada gaming regulators, creating what’s called a circuit split. In its petition, New Jersey said “[t]hat split has tremendous importance, as it will determine whether a multi-billion-dollar gaming industry can suddenly operate free from state sports-gaming laws.” Bloomberg Law noted that the Trump administration supports the prediction markets in these disputes, asserting that “it has sole oversight” of their offerings.

House squashes measure to prevent Supreme Court from expanding

Zachary Schermele, USA Today

On Wednesday, “Democrats in the House of Representatives batted down a longshot constitutional amendment to freeze the number of justices on the Supreme Court at nine,” according to USA Today. The vote was 212-206, “with only one Democrat, Rep. Don Davis of North Carolina, siding with Republicans.” The amendment “needed two-thirds support in the chamber to pass.” Rep. Andy Biggs, a Republican from Arizona, spoke in support of the amendment on the House floor before it failed. “We should not change the Supreme Court simply because we don’t like the people sitting on it,” he said.

State of Michigan responds to Americans for Citizen Voting appeal to US Supreme Court

Katherine Dailey, Michigan Advance

On Monday, the sponsors of a proposal for Michigan to impose a proof-of-citizenship requirement on voters asked the Supreme Court on its interim docket to require the state to put this proposal on the November ballot. They contend, among other things, “that the due process rights of Michiganders who signed the” petition to get the proposal on the ballot “were violated when the Board of State Canvassers determined that affidavits validating nine rejected signatures were submitted too late and as such could not be used to have those signatures – which would have put the petition over the threshold – count as valid.” On Wednesday, Michigan officials responded to the sponsors’ request, telling the justices “that the process of a referendum like this is a state-created right as opposed to one guaranteed by the First Amendment,” and is therefore not entitled to the same level of protection, according to Michigan Advance. “[M]any courts have held that private citizens lack a constitutional right to propose referenda or initiatives for any ballot, federal or state,” the officials asserted. They further argued that the sponsors have failed to account for “the high number of signatures that were found to be invalid.”

On Trump’s Ballroom, Chief Justice Finds Himself in an Unusual Spot: In Dissent

Ann E. Marimow, The New York Times

On Monday, the Supreme Court cleared the way for construction to continue on the new White House ballroom. Chief Justice John Roberts dissented, in an opinion joined by the court’s three Democratic appointees. The New York Times highlighted Roberts’ vote in an article about how rarely he is in dissent. “Since 2020, he has on average voted with the majority in argued cases that were not unanimous 91 percent of the time. Throughout his tenure, he has voted with the majority 83 percent of the time – the fifth highest of any justice and the highest of any chief justice since 1953, according to an analysis by Lee Epstein, a political scientist and law professor at Washington University in St. Louis.”

Maine’s high court rules father can restrict daughter’s church attendance

Sean Scott, The Maine Monitor

On Tuesday, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court ruled that “[a] Portland District Court judge was correct in giving a father the power to decide whether his daughter could attend an evangelical church following a clash with the girl’s mother over her religious upbringing.” The judge sided with Matthew Bradeen over Emily Bickford after determining that “some of the church’s language was ‘psychologically damaging the child,’” including teachings about “the rapture, a belief that Christians will join God at the end of the world and nonbelievers will be left behind,” according to The Maine Monitor. Bickford’s lawyer, Mathew Staver of Liberty Counsel, told The Monitor that they plan to appeal the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court. “I think it will be a case that will be very significant and catch the attention of the Supreme Court because of how far-reaching it is with regards to the First Amendment exercise clause,” Staver said.

On Site

From the SCOTUSblog Team

Why religion and education will be in the spotlight next term

By Kelsey Dallas

As the back-to-school spirit sweeps across the nation, education is likely on the minds of the Supreme Court justices (especially those with kids still at home or in college). The court is preparing for a term that will involve at least one major dispute on religion in schools – and potentially more.

SCOTUS Outside Opinions

How William Howard Taft transformed from a portly president to a svelte chief justice

By Jordan Lorence

In a column for SCOTUSblog, Jordan Lorence highlighted William Howard Taft’s physical transformation in the years after his left the White House, including during his time as chief justice. “People remember Taft as a heavy president, but few are aware that he lost a great deal of weight later in life when he headed the court,” Lorence wrote, exploring the healthy changes Taft made and what can be learned from “Taft-maxxing.”

Podcasts

Amarica's Constitution

The Statesman's Constitution - Special Guest Steven B. Smith

Originalists venerate the founders, who were by most reckonings a group of remarkable statesmen. Today, many Americans look seemingly in vain for a statesman worthy of the moment and its challenges. But what is a statesman? Does the Constitution assume a statesman will lead the country? Steven B. Smith, author of the new book On Statesmanship, joins to discuss.

A Closer Look

Woodward v. Alabama

On Sept. 28, 2006, Montgomery, Alabama, police officer Keith Houts was shot during a traffic stop. The shooter fled the scene, but investigators were able to quickly track down the car’s owner, Morrie Surles, because Houts had recorded the license plate before he was hit. Surles told the police that she bought the car for her daughter, Tiffany. The next day, Tiffany’s boyfriend, Mario Woodward, was arrested and charged with attempted murder. When Houts died from his injuries, the charges were upgraded to capital murder, and Woodward was ultimately found guilty and sentenced to death.

Woodward has spent much of his time on Alabama’s death row pursuing challenges to his conviction, filing three different petitions for review at the Supreme Court over the past 13 years. The first two were denied, and the third is scheduled to be considered by the justices during their “long conference” on Sept. 28. Woodward contends that it raises a significant question about state courts’ application of Brady v. Maryland, a major ruling on postconviction relief.

In Brady, which was argued and decided in 1963, the Supreme Court held that prosecutors’ decision to withhold evidence favorable to John Brady from his legal team violated Brady’s due process rights under the 14th Amendment. The ruling is the basis of what is now referred to as the Brady rule, under which prosecutors must share with the defense “any information favorable to the accused which may reduce a defendant’s potential sentence, go against the credibility of an unfavorable witness, or otherwise allow a jury to infer against the defendant’s guilt.” Defendants who identify a potential Brady violation after their conviction can file a challenge seeking to have the conviction overturned.

Woodward’s pending petition centers on a Brady claim he filed in 2023, after he obtained records related to the Houts shooting from the U.S. Marshals Service based on a Freedom of Information Act request. The records, though partially redacted, showed that officers had investigated a different, previously undisclosed suspect before zeroing in on Woodward. Woodward asserts that prosecutors violated Brady by failing to make his legal team aware of this alternative suspect.

The Circuit Court of Montgomery County and the Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals both denied Woodward’s 2023 claim, concluding that he had waited too long after receiving the records from the U.S. Marshals Service to seek postconviction relief and that he had failed to adequately explain how knowledge of the alternative suspect would have changed his defense strategy. “In particular,” according to the Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals’ ruling, “Woodward failed to plead any facts in his amended petition explaining whether the result of his trial would have been different had the alleged newly discovered evidence been known at the time of trial.”

In March, Woodward asked the Supreme Court to review the Alabama courts’ treatment of his Brady claim, contending that they “erroneously reformulated” Supreme Court precedent. Specifically, Woodward asserts that, under the Brady line of cases, he needed only to show that knowledge of the alternative suspect would have had a “probable impact” on his trial to be entitled to postconviction relief. The lower courts improperly held him to a higher standard, according to Woodward, expecting him to more definitively prove that his trial would have turned out differently. Woodward further argues that the lower courts misapplied the time limit by failing to acknowledge the time he spent waiting for the Marshals Service to confirm that the records were redacted correctly.

In its response to Woodward’s petition for review, Alabama asserts that Woodward failed to raise the issues in his petition before the lower courts, which means “the record is entirely undeveloped” and a poor candidate for Supreme Court review. The case is also not worthy of the court’s attention, according to the state, because it is “heavily factbound” and “presents no important federal question for the Court to answer and no conflict among the lower courts requiring resolution.”

As noted above, Woodward v. Alabama is scheduled to be considered by the justices for the first time on Sept. 28.

SCOTUS Quote

“The plea was not guilty, and he was convicted. No matter what the evidence was against him, he had the right to have an impartial judge.”

— Chief Justice William Howard Taft in Tumey v. Ohio (1927)

title: The Supreme Court Under Threat: Early Lessons in Judicial Self-Protection Harvard Law Review
author: @HarvLRev
content:
Because the Supreme Court is powerful, it is largely able to fulfill its legal responsibilities. Because it is a court — because it lacks both the sword and the purse — it is vulnerable to being defied successfully by Presidents and states and punished by Congress.

This Essay argues that the Court has become powerful despite being vulnerable because it has learned through hard experience to perform two roles reasonably well. The first is legal: The Court interprets and applies the Constitution and federal statutes in disputes before it. The second is political: The Court must survive in a world in which it ultimately must persuade powerful politicians to abide by its decisions. In short, the Court has two central tasks, especially when under threat — preserving the rule of law, and protecting itself. Commentators who believe that the Court should focus exclusively on its legal function fail to credit sufficiently the fact that, even today, the Court does not just act; it can also be acted upon — or ignored.

As this Essay shows, the Court began playing both roles early on. The Court made itself available to interpret and apply the law, as Article III of the Constitution and the Judiciary Act of 1789 directed. But the Court soon learned that it could not continue performing this legal function if it did not develop a way of practicing self-protective politics. Drawing upon several historical episodes, this Essay contends that the Supreme Court inevitably, and (within limits) properly, takes account of political threats to itself in exercising judicial review.

Part I identifies the reasons for the Court’s institutional vulnerability and the devices that the Court has developed over time to navigate difficult situations, including the current challenges facing the Court. Parts II through IV examine three episodes from the nineteenth century in which the Court successfully, although not always perfectly, navigated existential threats to its continued authority: cases arising out of the Jeffersonian backlash against the judiciary after the elections of 1800; Georgia’s defiance of the Court in the Cherokee Cases of the 1830s; and the Court’s decisions about military trials after the Civil War. The Conclusion defends the Court’s use of the tools of judicial self-protection despite the potential costs of such use.

title: In final scheduled summer order list, Supreme Court again declines to weigh in on COVID-19 vaccine mandate case
author: Amy Howe
content:
The Supreme Court on Friday morning once again declined to weigh in on a case brought by New York healthcare workers who were denied a religious accommodation from the state’s COVID-19 vaccine mandate for healthcare workers and lost their jobs when they were not vaccinated. The denial of rehearing in Does 1-2 v. Hochul came as part of the third and final regularly scheduled list of summer orders.

Summer order lists normally serve as a chance for the justices to clear out some of the pending requests for action – particularly petitions for rehearing – that build up between the end of June or early July, when they hold their final conference before their summer recess, and late September, when they return and hold the so-called “long conference.” Although the court ordinarily does not add new cases to its merits docket on its summer order lists (as opposed to after the “long conference”), it sometimes opts to do so, as it did on July 20, when it granted review in Jouppi v. Alaska.

In Does 1-2 v. Hochul, the court denied the healthcare workers’ original petition for review on June 29, over a dissent by Justice Neil Gorsuch that Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito joined. Gorsuch contended that the healthcare workers’ case “raises an important and recurring question of federal law that warrants this Court’s attention.” “I fail to see,” Gorsuch emphasized, “how a state law (especially an unconstitutional state law) prohibiting an accommodation can always and automatically supply an employer with a” defense that accommodating the employee’s religious observance or practice would place an “undue hardship” on the employer’s business.

On July 23, the healthcare workers asked the Supreme Court to reconsider its denial of review. They argued that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit, whose decision the Supreme Court had left in place, has continued to adhere to its position that “federal antidiscrimination claims must yield to contrary state statutory schemes.” Moreover, they added, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit has also “adopted the framework that religious accommodations must yield to contrary state laws,” which exacerbates the division among federal appeals courts on this question – an important factor that the Supreme Court considers in deciding whether to grant review.

On Friday, the court turned down the healthcare workers’ petition for reconsideration without asking New York Governor Kathy Hochul to respond.

The justices will meet on Sept. 28 for their “long conference”; they are likely to issue an initial list of orders from that conference later that week.

Model Compression

This section provides transparency about the compression state of each model available on our platform. We host a variety of open-source models from the community. We do not currently host pruned models on our public endpoints. All models served through our public endpoints are the original, unpruned versions. While we conduct research on pruning techniques like REAP (Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning), these pruned models are shared with the research community on Hugging Face but are not available through our shared API. You can read more about REAP in our research blog. All of our public models are unpruned. Cerebras uses selective weight-only quantization only during storage to preserve maximal quality. This means that the weights are stored in partial 16-bit / 8-bit / 4-bit, in-line with industry standards. For quality, sensitive layers are stored at full precision with dequantization on the fly, so operations are done in high precision. The activations, attention, and kv cache remain in full precision and unquantized.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will you change a model's architecture without notice?

No. We are committed to serving the original models for all existing endpoints, without modification. We do not alter model architectures via pruning on our hosted portfolio. If we explore additional compression techniques (like pruning) in the future, these would be offered as separate endpoints with pruning-specific names, ensuring complete transparency and allowing you to choose which version best fits your needs.

Where can I find your REAP pruned models?

Our REAP pruned models are available on Hugging Face for research and experimentation purposes: Cerebras REAP Collection. These models demonstrate our pruning research but are not served through our production API.

What are compression, quantization, and pruning?

Compression is an umbrella term for techniques that reduce model size or computational requirements. Common compression techniques include:

  • Quantization: Reducing the precision of numbers used to represent model weights (e.g., converting from FP16 to FP8). This reduces memory usage without changing the model’s architecture.
  • Pruning: Permanently removing parts of a model, like layers or experts, to reduce model size. This changes the model’s architecture and creates a different model.
